name: Special Education and Accessibility
blurb: A review of research on AI with students with disabilities found something uncomfortable. Much of the work described AI as a way to relieve adults of the burden of working with these students, rather than as a way to empower the students and their families (Rice, 2023).
title: Special Education and Accessibility
answer: A review of research on AI with students with disabilities found something uncomfortable. Much of the work described AI as a way to relieve adults of the burden of working with these students, rather than as a way to empower the students and their families (Rice, 2023).

papers.why: Human-like avatars can import bias into AI tutoring.
papers.title: Face value: How avatar identity shapes epistemic trust in AI-mediated learning
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Two experiments (N=102, N=294): AI tutor avatar race, gender, and age shaped credibility and whether learners used the guidance. White avatars, and Asian male avatars in STEM, were rated more credible; older Black female avatars were penalized. STEM tasks amplified bias.

papers.title: Intervention Fidelity for Enhanced Outcomes: A Systematic Review of Artificial Intelligence in Special Education
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: Five studies: AI tools were associated with better intervention fidelity monitoring; links to student outcomes are indirect.

papers.why: Balances accommodation vs skill-building for students with LD.
papers.title: Cognitive Offloading in the Age of Generative AI: What Does It Mean for Students With Learning Disabilities?
papers.finding: Conceptual review: GenAI can compensate for learning disabilities but excessive offloading may bypass needed skills; proposes strategic offloading model.

papers.why: Suggests structured AI writing support can help students with LD.
papers.title: AI-assisted writing and the impact of ChatGPT on Greek-speaking students with and without learning disabilities. Outcomes from a repeated measures design
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: First-year teacher education students including some with learning disabilities: structured instruction in AI-assisted writing improved writing quality; students with learning difficulties gained most in performance and self-efficacy.

papers.why: AI in class does not close SES gaps; teach digital skills explicitly.
papers.title: Decoding divides: The role of socioeconomic status and personality traits in AI divides and educational inequality
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: 4,497 Dutch Grade 6 students: digital literacy, not amount of AI use, mediated links between personality traits and achievement. Family SES advantage was direct and not changed by classroom AI use.

papers.why: Default AI output can burden DHH students; accessibility needs explicit prompting.
papers.title: Exploring the design of LLM-powered question generation for deaf and hard of hearing learners
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: LLM-generated quiz questions for Deaf and Hard of Hearing learners often used compound sentences, double negatives, and complex clauses; customized prompts and guidance were needed. Framed with Language Deprivation Theory.

papers.why: Design notes for girls-in-computing AI programs.
papers.title: Beyond “painting in pink”: A critical case study of all-girls generative AI workshops in a European makerspace and implications for gender equity in computing
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: All-girls GenAI makerspace workshops: representation, relationship building, and responsive teaching supported girls; challenges included poor topic choice and limited peer interaction.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence to Support Writing Outcomes for Students With Disabilities
papers.finding: Crosswalk of AI writing tools to NAEP writing criteria for struggling writers; conceptual.

papers.title: The Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence-Based Interventions for Students with Learning Disabilities: A Systematic Review
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 11 studies, 3,033 students with learning disabilities: all reported positive results, but none rated low risk of bias.

papers.title: The effectiveness of AI-assisted instruction for primary school students with mathematics learning disabilities
papers.venue: Psychology, Evaluation, and Technology in Educational Research
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment, 42 grade 3 to 5 students with math learning disabilities, 12 weeks: achievement d = 0.89, motivation d = 0.76.

papers.why: Students with disabilities are rarely studied; text-only design excludes some.
papers.title:
Exploring Artificial Intelligence Integration and Student‐
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Interaction in K‐12 Education: A Scoping Review
papers.finding: Scoping review of 70 K-12 student-AI studies (2014-2023): few reported student diversity; chatbots and tutors dominate; input is mostly single-modality text.

papers.title: Let's CHAT About Artificial Intelligence for Students With Disabilities: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.caveat: Pooled effects hide variation across settings.
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 29 (quasi-)experiments with students with disabilities: medium effect, g = 0.588; no significant moderators.

papers.title: The effectiveness of using artificial intelligence in improving academic skills of school-aged students with mild intellectual disabilities in Saudi Arabia
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 70 boys aged 9 to 12 with mild intellectual disability, ten 60-minute AI-personalized sessions over 5 weeks: gains on Woodcock-Johnson IV held at one month. Effect sizes unusually large.

papers.why: Connects GenAI to Universal Design for Learning.
papers.title: Harnessing the Power of Generative AI to Support ALL Learners
papers.finding: Summer 2023 teacher institute: most teachers had never used GenAI; 43% believed it would make instruction more accessible for all learners; UDL strategies for English learners and students with disabilities.

papers.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence with Students with Identified Disabilities: A Systematic Review with Critique
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: Slim research base; AI often framed as relieving adults of the burden of working with students with disabilities rather than empowering students and families.

papers.title: Partnering with immigrant families to promote language justice and equity in education
papers.finding: Focus groups with Spanish, Portuguese, and Cantonese-speaking families: poor interpretation reduced access to special education services and trust in schools.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in special education: a systematic review
papers.finding: Review of 29 studies (2008-2020) on AI in special education: mostly US, autism focus, technical rather than educational models.

papers.title: Assistive technology for the inclusion of students with disabilities: a systematic review
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 31 studies: assistive technology increases inclusion and access; barriers are teacher training, information, and accessibility.

children.name: Drafting IEP Goals With Names Removed
children.blurb: Drafting IEP goals with names removed means using an AI tool, such as the IEP features in MagicSchool, to produce a first draft of a goal from the skill, the student's current level and the general context, with no identifying details entered.

children.name: Plain Language Summaries for Families
children.blurb: A plain language summary turns key parts of an IEP into a short explanation families can understand, using an approved tool with names removed.

children.name: Progress Monitoring and Fidelity
children.blurb: Progress monitoring and fidelity means tracking whether a student is moving toward their goals and checking whether the planned interventions are actually being delivered.

children.name: Compliance and Scheduling
children.blurb: Compliance and scheduling in special education means using management and scheduling software, including AI features, to track legal deadlines and arrange related services.

children.name: Accommodation Alerts for Every Teacher
children.blurb: Accommodation alerts for every teacher means using student information systems and AI to give each teacher short, clear notes about the accommodations a student requires.

children.name: Accessibility in Every Classroom
children.blurb: Accessibility in every classroom means making tools such as live captions, text to speech, dictation, and image descriptions available to all students, not only those with disabilities.

children.name: Assistive Technology and Communication
children.blurb: Assistive technology can change a student's education when the right tool is matched to the right student.

children.name: Executive Function and Behavior Support
children.blurb: Executive function and behavior support means using AI to help students with disabilities plan, organize, and manage time, and to help staff create visual schedules, social narratives, and behavior data charts.

children.name: Structured Writing Support
children.blurb: Structured writing support means teaching students to use AI at specific stages of writing, such as organizing ideas before writing or getting feedback on a draft, while they do the writing themselves.

children.name: Transition Planning
children.blurb: Transition planning prepares students with disabilities for life after high school, including further education, work and independent living, and federal regulations require it in the IEP that will be in effect when a student turns 16.

children.name: Accessible Assessment and Adaptive Practice
children.blurb: Accessible assessment means making tests measure what a student knows rather than their disability, with AI helping teachers create versions that use simpler language, larger print, audio, or different formats as allowed by a student's IEP.

children.name: Privacy for Students With Disabilities
children.blurb: Privacy for students with disabilities means treating evaluation results, diagnoses and behavior records as among the most sensitive information a school holds, and keeping identifying details away from any AI tool that is not covered by a signed data privacy agreement.

children.name: Supporting the Adults Who Support Students
children.blurb: This idea is about using AI to support the adults around special education students, especially paraprofessionals and new teachers, while keeping human review in place.

children.name: What the Case Manager and Team Decide
children.blurb: In special education, the IEP team, including parents, decides eligibility, goals, services, and placement, and no AI tool may make those decisions.

sections.body: Special education and accessibility is the part of school life where students with disabilities receive services, supports, and tools that help them learn and take part. The book says AI is already doing several concrete things here, such as speech tools, captions, image descriptions, and communication devices that open doors, and drafting tools that can give special education staff back hours now spent on paperwork. It also covers the individualized education program process, parent communication, progress monitoring and compliance, accessibility tools for every classroom, assistive technology and communication devices, executive function and behavior support, transition planning, and accessible assessment. The book warns that a review titled The Use of Artificial Intelligence with Students with Identified Disabilities: A Systematic Review with Critique found much of the work framed AI as a way to relieve adults of the burden of working with these students rather than to empower students and families, and that the research base is slim. Figure 12.2 maps the ideas and their evidence, with two ideas carrying moderate evidence and most of the rest described as practices to pilot with care.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, in the book's account, is AI that gives students with disabilities real access and gives staff time to spend more of it with students and families. The meta-analysis titled Let's CHAT About Artificial Intelligence for Students With Disabilities: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis found a medium sized positive effect of AI on learning for these students, and speech tools, captions, image descriptions, and communication devices open doors that were closed a generation ago. What does not work is the pre written individualized education program, where a case manager uses AI to draft goals and services, brings a polished document to the meeting, and the family feels the decisions were made before they arrived, so the meeting becomes a formality and the program reflects a template rather than a real conversation about a real child. The rule the book holds to is that decisions about a student's education stay with a team that includes the family, that individualized education program drafts are treated as proposals, that families receive plain language summaries they can check against the full individualized education program, and that the human review rule, with Figure 12.4 adopted as part of it, covers every special education decision. Student names and details stay out of any AI tool not covered by a signed agreement, and the time saved should be used to give staff more time with students and families rather than to move through paperwork and meetings faster.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as a path from drafting and family communication to monitoring, compliance, classroom access, and the final team decision. A teacher would go to Accommodation Alerts for Every Teacher and Accessibility in Every Classroom for everyday access, to Assistive Technology and Communication for devices and communication support, to Executive Function and Behavior Support for regulation and behavior, to Structured Writing Support for writing help, and to Accessible Assessment and Adaptive Practice for testing and practice that fit the student. A leader would go to Drafting IEP Goals With Names Removed and Privacy for Students With Disabilities to keep drafting and data safe, to Progress Monitoring and Fidelity and Compliance and Scheduling to check that services are delivered and documented, and to Supporting the Adults Who Support Students to protect the staff who carry this work. A parent would go to Plain Language Summaries for Families to check the full individualized education program in words they can use, to Transition Planning for the move beyond school, and to What the Case Manager and Team Decide to see where their voice belongs in the decision. Read together, these pages keep the purpose in view, that AI should serve the student and the family, not replace the team's thinking.
